newsitem.title: USA: Key House Democrat to offer power bill next week.
newsitem.headline: Key House Democrat to offer power bill next week.

text.p: U.S. Rep. Ed Markey said Wednesday he planned to reintroduce a bill next week that would offer states incentives to open local power markets to competition.
The Massachusetts Democrat's bill would be the third major electricity restructuring plan to be offered in the House this year.

Markey, an influential member of the House Commerce Committee, warned that while lawmakers had sat through several hearings on electricity restructuring, they were unlikely to be able to pass a bill in July, as planned by energy and power panel chairman Rep. Dan Schaefer, a Colorado Republican.

"I do not believe ... that it is realistic to move to a Subcommittee markup in July absent a breakthrough that significantly advances the prospects of achieving a bipartisan consensus," he said at a conference sponsored by Energy Daily.

Unlike the two Republican electric restructuring bills, which seek to set a deadline for states to offer all consumers a choice of power suppliers, Markey's legislation would not force states to open their markets.

Instead, it would exempt utilities from the Public Utility Holding Company Act (PUHCA) and the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act (PURPA) if the states where they operate deregulate their markets.
Investor-owned utilities have long pressed Congress to repeal PUHCA and PURPA, saying the two laws limit their ability to compete with independent power producers.

PUHCA restricts utility holding companies from investing in other businesses, including natural gas firms, in order to protect investors from subsidizing unprofitable ventures outside a utility's main line of business.

PURPA requires utilities to buy a certain amount of power from independent power producers which use renewable energy or cogeneration. Many long-term PURPA contracts were priced far above current market levels.

In a bid to address concerns about utility mergers and market concentration, Markey said his bill would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and states more authority to prevent anticompetitive actions.

On the key issue of stranded costs, he said states should be allowed to determine how much of their unprofitable investment costs utilities should be allowed to recoup from customers in the transition to an open market.

"The states are in a better position than federal regulators to judge the extent to which they were lied to, mislead or simply credulous when they approved the utilities' original investments in nuclear power plants or long-term PURPA contracts," Markey said.
